extracted.intended_audience: general readers; public speakers, essayists, and conversationalists
extracted.subtask_description: Advice and evaluative principles (from a 19th‑century essay) about preparing and delivering lectures, choosing conversational topics, handling audiences and societies, and literary honesty/originality. Useful for public speaking and informal writing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Popular lecture accessibility
rubrics_metrics.description: "A thoroughly popular lecture ought to have nothing in it which five hundred people cannot all take in a flash, just as it is uttered.",
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make lectures immediately comprehensible to a large audience; avoid points that require prolonged reflection or explanation — aim for instant grasp by a crowd.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lecture should interest everyone and be widely understandable
rubrics_metrics.description: "A lecture ought to be something which all can understand, about something which interests everybody.",
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose subject matter with broad appeal and present it in clear language so the widest possible audience finds it engaging and intelligible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Talk on long‑held subjects; listen on newly studied ones
rubrics_metrics.description: "Talk about those subjects you have had long in your mind, and listen to what others say about subjects you have studied but recently.",
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Speak on topics you've long reflected on (depth and ease of delivery), and reserve recent/less‑seasoned topics for listening and learning rather than exposition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Season knowledge before using it publicly
rubrics_metrics.description: "Knowledge and timber shouldn’t be much used, till they are seasoned.",
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid displaying fresh, untested facts or arguments; let ideas 'season' through thought and experience before presenting them to audiences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Repetition and age improve lectures
rubrics_metrics.description: "A new lecture is just like any other new tool... A lecture doesn’t begin to be old until it has passed its hundredth delivery... These old lectures are a man’s best, commonly; they improve by age...",
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practice and repeated delivery refine timing, remove dead spots, and make material more effective; keep working a lecture rather than abandoning it and returning later (which can reintroduce blisters/loathing).

rubrics_metrics.name: Adapt material to audience — trade depth for effect
rubrics_metrics.description: "One learns to make the most of their strong points and to carry off their weak ones,—to take out the really good things which don’t tell on the audience, and put in cheaper things that do. All this degrades him, of course, but it improves the lecture for general delivery.",
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When addressing general audiences, emphasize elements that register with listeners even if it means simplifying or omitting subtler material; accept some artistic compromise to increase communicative impact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Target the most responsive audience members
rubrics_metrics.description: "Front seats: ... Bright women’s faces, young and middle‑aged, a little behind these, but toward the front—(pick out the best, and lecture mainly to that.)",
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While addressing a mixed audience, focus delivery toward the attentive, sympathetic subset (those whose responses you can read) — their engagement will guide and buoy the overall performance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expect uniform audience reactions; plan timing accordingly
rubrics_metrics.description: "Each audience laughs, and each cries, in just the same places of your lecture; that is, if you make one laugh or cry, you make all.",
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize predictable collective responses and time jokes, anecdotes, and emotional passages where audiences typically react; reliable cues recur across different assemblies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not let 'men of facts' crush conversation
rubrics_metrics.description: "When a person is really full of information, and does not abuse it to crush conversation, his part is to that of the real talkers what the instrumental accompaniment is in a trio or quartette of vocalists.",
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In conversation or panels, supply factual ballast without dominating or shutting down discussion; use facts to support, not to overpower, the flow of ideas and social interaction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conversational roles — the questioner vs. the 'Bylaws' member
rubrics_metrics.description: (satirical) "There are two espèces d’individus qu’on trouve toujours à ces Sociétés: 1° Le membre à questions; 2° Le membre à 'Bylaws.' ... Le faiseur de questions donne peu d’attention aux réponses... Le membre à 'Bylaws' ... C’est sa religion; ... C’est la CONSTITUTION!",
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be aware of recurring unhelpful participant types in societies/meetings: the perennial questioner (seeks attention rather than answers) and the pedantic rule‑monger (fixated on procedure). Manage or moderate their influence to preserve useful discourse.

rubrics_metrics.name: On originality and plagiarism — disclaim or acknowledge coincidences
rubrics_metrics.description: "I think few persons have a greater disgust for plagiarism than myself... If I had even suspected that the idea in question was borrowed, I should have disclaimed originality, or mentioned the coincidence... I do therefore... relinquish all claim to being considered the _first_ person who gave utterance to a certain simile...",
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exercise literary honesty: if an idea may plausibly be borrowed or coincident with another's, acknowledge it or disclaim originality; avoid asserting sole authorship when uncertain.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reader’s response can and should transcend the author’s text
rubrics_metrics.description: "The suggested trains of thought and feeling ought always to rise above—not the author, but the reader’s mental version of the author, whoever he may be.",
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim for writing that stimulates readers to develop thoughts and feelings beyond the literal text and their prior conception of the author; value the reader’s imaginative expansion as a mark of success.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer life’s experience over books for humanity in discourse
rubrics_metrics.description: "I always believed in life rather than in books... every day of earth... has more of humanity in it than all the books that were ever written, put together.",
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ground lectures and conversation in lived experience and human particulars rather than relying solely on bookish quotation or abstract erudition; vivid life‑based material resonates more strongly with audiences.
